analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a 17% flat tax on wages and business income, repeals the estate tax and all tax credits.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced April 7, 2017 with zero cosponsors, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would throw out the current income tax and replace it with a single 17% rate. Only wages, retirement payouts, and unemployment benefits would count as income, taxed after a large standard deduction. Capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances would not be taxed at all, and every federal income tax credit — including the Earned Income Tax Credit and the Child Tax Credit — would be repealed. It would also repeal the estate and gift taxes, loosen most pension protections, let employers pull money back out of overfunded pension plans without the usual penalty tax, and require a three-fifths vote of Congress to ever change these tax rates.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: their capital gains, dividends, and interest would go untaxed, the alternative minimum tax would disappear, and the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes would be repealed entirely. Businesses gain by being taxed only on active business income. Some low earners gain from a larger standard deduction. Employers with overfunded pensions gain the right to reclaim surplus assets, paying ordinary income tax but no penalty.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the multiple income tax brackets with one 17% rate on taxable income, and defines taxable income simply as wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation minus a standard deduction, which would make filing much simpler.
Sets a large standard deduction — $14,590 for singles and $29,190 for joint filers in 2017, adjusted for inflation — so some low-wage earners would owe little or nothing.
Repeals the alternative minimum tax, which many middle- and upper-middle-income families pay in high-tax, high-cost areas.
Replaces the corporate tax with a 17% tax on the business taxable income of any person or firm doing business in the United States, with simple deductions for inputs and cash wages.
Repeals estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes for deaths and gifts after December 31, 2017.

analysis.who_pays: Working families lose the Earned Income Tax Credit, Child Tax Credit, and every other income tax credit, since the bill repeals them all. Households whose income is mostly wages face the full 17% rate with no credits to offset it. Employees of tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local governments would see a 17% tax on the value of their noncash benefits like health coverage, paid by their employer. Pension plan protections for lower-paid workers disappear, and the federal Treasury would forgo revenue from the estate tax and untaxed investment income.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals all income tax credits, including the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, which would raise taxes on millions of low- and middle-income working families even as the rate drops to 17%.

Only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation count as income, so capital gains, dividends, and interest would go completely untaxed — a large benefit flowing to households that live on investment income.
It repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, which fall almost entirely on the largest inheritances.

It repeals pension nondiscrimination rules, minimum coverage requirements, and contribution limits, removing rules that require retirement plans to benefit rank-and-file workers and not just executives, and it repeals the penalty on early retirement-plan withdrawals.

It repeals the excise tax on employer reversions of pension surplus, letting employers pull excess assets out of defined-benefit plans and pay only normal income tax — a transfer of pension surpluses to company balance sheets.

Title II makes it out of order for Congress to consider any bill that raises a tax rate, creates a rate, cuts the standard deduction, or reduces revenue, waivable only by a three-fifths vote — locking the new tax structure in against ordinary legislative majorities.

Employees of tax-exempt organizations and of federal, state, and local governments would face a new 17% employer-paid tax on the value of noncash compensation such as health benefits, discouraging those benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real: one rate, one big deduction, no AMT, and a far shorter tax code would save many households real time and money. But the distribution is lopsided. Wage earners — the vast majority of Americans — pay the full 17% with no credits, while investment income and inheritances go untaxed and the largest estates are freed from the estate tax. Independent analyses of similar flat-tax proposals have generally projected large revenue losses, which would have to be made up elsewhere or add to deficits. Repealing pension nondiscrimination rules and letting companies reclaim pension surpluses without penalty shifts value from rank-and-file retirement security toward employers. A modest simplification gain is bought at the price of a large upward shift in who pays.

outcome.mechanism: Shelby introduced the bill and the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or a vote; it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the SMART Act on April 7, 2017, and the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill.
The action history shows no further action after the committee referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee without ever being considered.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly from a bill that was never considered; the existing tax code, with its credits, progressive rates, and estate tax, simply remained in place. To the extent anyone benefited, it was the status quo — including working families who would have lost the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit under this bill.

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor: introduced the flat tax bill on April 7, 2017.

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill received no action after referral for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: No senator cosponsored the bill and the Senate never voted on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; a single Republican introduced the bill, no one from either party cosponsored it, and the Republican-run Finance Committee never took it up.

industries.note: The bill untaxes capital gains, dividends, interest, and inheritances entirely, and repeals the estate tax, while taxing wages at a flat 17% with no credits. The households that gain the most are those with the most investment income and the largest estates.

industries.industry: Employers with overfunded defined-benefit pension plans
industries.note: Repealing the reversion excise tax lets employers pull surplus pension assets back onto their own balance sheets, paying only ordinary income tax. Accrued benefits are protected by vesting rules, but the surplus that funded them leaves workers' plans.

Repealing nondiscrimination, coverage, and contribution rules frees plans from compliance costs and lets plans skew toward highly paid employees, but the bill also imposes its own compliance questions and taxes noncash benefits at tax-exempt and government employers.

industries.industry: Tax-exempt organizations and governments as employers
industries.note: A new 17% tax falls on the value of noncash compensation — including health benefits — that these employers provide, a cost for-profits do not face for the same benefits.
